notes: \cpara{Opens with a causal story and calls it obvious. ``So obvious as to be worth belaboring'' is followed by no belaboring: three sentences, no evidence that ancestral arguments got people killed, and none that today's arguments run on that machinery.}

\cpara{The actual advice, and the only part of the essay that is argued at all. It carries two escape clauses: ``if you can possibly avoid it'' and ``unless all the discussants are already rational.'' The second undoes the rule, because any group that wants to discuss politics can count itself rational.}

\cpara{Three claims, none supported: politics is war, arguments are soldiers, and scientists turn into ``slogan-chanting zombies.'' The paragraph describes other people's tribalism in the voice of someone outside it.}

\cpara{The example is misstated. With ``All Quakers are pacifists'' and ``All Republicans are not pacifists,'' the premises contradict each other as soon as Nixon belongs to both classes. That is a contradiction in ordinary logic, not a problem in nonmonotonic reasoning. The standard version uses defaults: ``usually, Quakers are pacifist; usually, Republicans are not pacifist'' (Wikipedia, ``Nixon diamond''). The essay's version removes the feature the example exists to illustrate.}

\cpara{Accuses an unnamed author of choosing the example to make Republicans feel unwelcome. No author is named, and none is identified: according to Wikipedia, the first version, by Reiter and Criscuolo (1981), used a man named John. The plain reason for using Nixon, that he was a well-known real person who was both a Quaker and a Republican, is not considered. The questions are rhetorical, and the next paragraph supplies the answer without evidence.}

\cpara{Attributes a motive, hedged with ``probably'' (``couldn't resist getting in a good, solid dig''), to a person the essay cannot name. The essay does to the example's author what it tells readers not to do: it takes a dig at an imagined opponent, and the dig is about motives.}
\cpara{The advice at last, and its stated reason is the community's comfort, not accuracy (see the Response). ``Spiritual growth of the community'' is the goal, and it is never defined.}
